classification.difficultyReason: Eliminate the two radicals to construct a monic integer polynomial with constant term 1, then exclude its only possible rational roots for general positive n.

content.prompt: Let $x=\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n+1}$, where $n$ is a natural number. Prove that $x$ is irrational.

answer.short:
$x$ is irrational.

It is a root of the monic integer polynomial $P(t)=t^4-2(2n+1)t^2+1$. Its only possible rational roots are $\pm1$, but $P(1)=P(-1)=-4n\ne0$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=n+2\sqrt{n(n+1)}+n+1\\x^2&=2n+1+2\sqrt{n(n+1)}\\x^2-(2n+1)&=2\sqrt{n(n+1)}\\\bigl[x^2-(2n+1)\bigr]^2&=4n(n+1)\\x^4-2(2n+1)x^2+(2n+1)^2&=4n(n+1)\\x^4-2(2n+1)x^2+4n^2+4n+1&=4n^2+4n\\x^4-2(2n+1)x^2+1&=0\end{align*}$$
Let $P(t)=t^4-2(2n+1)t^2+1$. This is a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. By the Integer Root Theorem, its only possible rational roots are the integer factors of $1$, namely $1$ and $-1$.
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=1-2(2n+1)+1\\P(1)&=-4n\ne0\\P(-1)&=1-2(2n+1)+1\\P(-1)&=-4n\ne0\end{align*}$$
Since $n\ge1$, neither candidate is a root. Therefore $P$ has no rational roots, so $x$ is irrational.
